description: Why-questions across the human lifespan: studies and hormones. Request (translated from the German original, 2026-08-27): Children at a certain age ask many 'why?' questions. Adults do this less, which was presumably selected by evolution, because if adults also asked too many 'why?' questions they would neglect food gathering and starve. The further a society develops, the more 'why?' questions it can afford. The evolutionary selection pressure, however, is likely to be small. Which studies exist in this context and which hormones play a role? Compile the data as JSON in English and repeat this request in the description. Sourced findings are tagged 'measured value'; the two conjectures from the dialogue (foraging-time hypothesis, prosperity hypothesis) and the competing explanations are tagged 'assumed value' with a confidence number. All DOIs were verified on 2026-08-27.

triples.name: childhood is part of life history
child question rate
triples.description: questions per hour asked by engaged preschool children at home; Chouinard 2007, four children aged 1-5 from the CHILDES corpus.

triples.name: information-seeking question share
triples.description: share of children's questions to parents that seek information rather than attention, permission or help; Chouinard 2007.

triples.name: brain glucose share of resting metabolic rate
triples.description: brain glucose uptake expressed as share of the body's resting metabolic rate; Kuzawa et al. 2014, PET/MRI data from birth to adulthood.

triples.name: brain glucose share of daily energy requirement
brain glucose use peak
triples.description: the age at which brain glucose demand is maximal; it lies in childhood, not at birth, and coincides with slowest body growth.

triples.name: juvenile dependence duration
triples.description: years during which hunter-gatherer offspring are energetically subsidized by adults; embodied capital model (Kaplan et al. 2000).

triples.name: hunting productivity peak
triples.description: age of peak hunting return; Koster et al. 2020, ~23,000 hunting records, high skill is maintained through much of adulthood.

triples.name: curiosity influences memory
triples.description: high state curiosity improves memory for the curiosity-target and for incidental material, immediately and after one day; associated with anticipatory activity in midbrain and nucleus accumbens and midbrain-hippocampus coupling (Gruber et al. 2014).

triples.name: dopamine influences curiosity
triples.description: curiosity states engage the dopaminergic midbrain-accumbens-hippocampus circuit (Gruber et al. 2014, fMRI, correlational); Dubois et al. 2021 found no effect of the D2/D3 antagonist amisulpride on value-free random exploration, so dopamine's role is in valued, reward-anticipating curiosity rather than in cheap random sampling.

triples.name: noradrenaline influences random exploration
triples.description: 40 mg propranolol attenuated value-free random exploration in a double-blind placebo-controlled bandit study; amisulpride did not (Dubois et al. 2021).

triples.name: cortisol influences overexploitation
triples.description: higher cortisol response to an acute stressor and higher chronic stress scores predicted staying too long at depleting patches in a virtual foraging task (Lenow et al. 2017).

triples.name: stress influences exploitation
triples.description: acute and chronic stress shift foraging-like choices toward exploitation, i.e. away from sampling alternatives (Lenow et al. 2017).

triples.name: aging influences trait curiosity
triples.description: trait curiosity and novelty seeking decline with age; preserved curiosity is associated with better cognitive, emotional and physical outcomes, with dopaminergic and noradrenergic mechanisms proposed (Sakaki et al. 2018).

triples.name: aging influences state curiosity
triples.description: state curiosity for specific trivia questions increases across adulthood while trait curiosity declines (Whatley et al. 2025), so the adult decline is not uniform across curiosity types.

triples.name: explore-exploit trade-off influences adult question decline
triples.description: life-history explanation: the protected, adult-subsidized childhood is an evolved explore phase of broad hypothesis search; goal-directed exploitation sets in later (Gopnik 2020). Under this view the adaptation is the long childhood, not a suppression of adult questioning.

triples.name: knowledge gap closure influences adult question decline
triples.description: developmental explanation: questions are triggered by gaps, ambiguities and inconsistencies in current knowledge (Chouinard 2007; Frazier et al. 2009); as knowledge structures approach adult states fewer triggers occur.

triples.name: foraging influences adult question decline
triples.description: the foraging-time hypothesis from the dialogue. Counter-evidence: hunter-gatherer skill and productivity keep rising until the early-to-mid 30s (Koster et al. 2020), i.e. adult learning remains adaptive for decades; the cost that selection visibly acted on is the energetic cost of the childhood brain, not adult question time.

triples.name: prosperity influences question rate
triples.description: the prosperity hypothesis from the dialogue. Indirect support: children of lower socio-economic status ask fewer questions (Chouinard 2007 discussion; Kurkul and Corriveau 2018), and stress reduces exploration (Lenow et al. 2017); no direct cross-societal measurement of adult why-question rates was found.

triples.name: selection pressure on adult question decline
triples.description: the dialogue's own assessment that direct selection against adult questioning is weak; consistent with the literature, which attributes the pattern to life-history timing and development rather than to a selected adult trait.
